title: The Hand the Body Wants
paragraphs: Your two hands look nearly identical, yet no amount of turning will make a left hand fit a right glove.
Molecules can have the same property: one that cannot be superimposed on its own mirror image is called chiral, from the Greek word for hand, a term the physicist Lord Kelvin introduced in the 1890s.
In medicine, handedness turned out to be a matter of life and death, and later, a matter of marketing.
The story begins in Paris in 1848 with Louis Pasteur, then in his mid-twenties.
Chemists already knew that tartaric acid, obtained from the crust inside wine casks, rotated plane-polarized light, light filtered so that its waves vibrate in a single plane.
A second form, chemically identical in every test, did not rotate the light at all, and no one could say why.
Pasteur crystallized a sodium ammonium salt of the inactive acid and, examining the crystals under a magnifying lens, noticed that they came in two shapes that were mirror images of each other.
With tweezers he sorted them into two piles, dissolved each separately, and found that one solution rotated light to the right and the other to the left by the same amount.
The inactive acid was not inactive at all; it was an equal mixture of two opposite forms whose effects cancelled.
Such a fifty-fifty mixture is now called racemic.
The explanation came in 1874, when Jacobus van 't Hoff and Joseph Le Bel independently proposed that the four bonds of a carbon atom point toward the corners of a tetrahedron.
If the four attached groups are all different, they can be arranged in two ways that are mirror images and cannot be interconverted without breaking a bond.
Such a carbon is called a stereocenter, and the two mirror-image molecules are called enantiomers.
Enantiomers are strange twins.
They share the same melting point, boiling point, solubility, and density, and ordinary laboratory methods cannot tell them apart.
They differ in exactly two circumstances: in the direction they rotate polarized light, and in how they interact with other chiral things.
The nose makes the point vividly: one enantiomer of carvone smells of spearmint while its mirror image smells of caraway.
This matters in medicine because the body is itself overwhelmingly one-handed.
Proteins are built from amino acids of a single handedness, so every enzyme and every receptor is a chiral pocket, as particular about shape as a glove.

In 1933 the researchers Easson and Stedman offered a model still taught today: if a drug must touch its receptor at three points, only one enantiomer can line up all three at once, while its mirror image can manage two at best.
Pharmacologists call the better-fitting enantiomer the eutomer and its partner the distomer.
A distomer may do nothing, may do something milder, may do something different, or, in the worst case, may do harm.
The worst case has a name.
Thalidomide went on sale in West Germany in 1957 as a sedative and was soon taken by pregnant women for morning sickness.
By 1961 physicians had linked it to a wave of severe birth defects, often malformed or missing limbs, and it was withdrawn late that year.
Thousands of children were affected worldwide, by common estimates near ten thousand.

The United States was largely spared because Frances Kelsey, a reviewer at the Food and Drug Administration, refused to approve the drug for lack of adequate safety data; a 1962 law then strengthened the agency's demands for evidence.
Thalidomide has one stereocenter, and later animal studies indicated that one enantiomer carries the sedative effect while the other causes the birth defects.
It is tempting to conclude that selling only the safe hand would have averted the tragedy, but that conclusion is wrong.

The hydrogen on thalidomide's stereocenter is easily removed and replaced under the mild conditions of the bloodstream, so either pure enantiomer turns into a mixture of both within hours of being swallowed.
A single-enantiomer thalidomide would not have been a safe drug, because the body would have manufactured the harmful form on its own.
The drug has since returned under strict controls, approved by the FDA in 1998 for a painful complication of leprosy and later for a cancer of the bone marrow.
Ibuprofen tells a gentler version of the same story.
Developed at the Boots company in Britain in the 1960s, it has mainly been sold as a racemate.
Only the S enantiomer blocks the enzyme that produces the signaling molecules behind pain and inflammation; the R enantiomer is nearly inert at that target.

Instead the body attaches the R form to a carrier molecule, inverts its stereocenter, and releases it as the active S form, a conversion that runs in only one direction and captures a large share of the R form, by many estimates more than half.
The supposedly inactive half of the tablet is in effect a slow-release supply of the active one.
A pure S version is sold in some countries, but the racemate remains the standard.
In 1992 the FDA issued a policy statement encouraging developers to study each enantiomer of a new chiral drug separately, and single enantiomers became the norm for new chiral medicines.
The more interesting development was commercial.
A company whose racemic drug was nearing the end of its patent could isolate the eutomer and launch it as a new product under a new patent, a maneuver the industry calls a chiral switch.
The most famous example is esomeprazole, the S enantiomer of the stomach-acid drug omeprazole, approved in the United States in 2001 as the older drug's patent protection was running out.
Advertised directly to consumers as the purple pill, it went on to sell billions of dollars' worth a year.
Here is where a careful reader should slow down.
Omeprazole is a prodrug: it does nothing until it reaches the acid-secreting cells of the stomach lining, where acid converts it into an active form that has no stereocenter at all.
At the site of action, in other words, the two enantiomers become the same molecule.
The difference lies in the liver, which breaks down the S enantiomer more slowly, so a given dose of esomeprazole delivers somewhat more drug to the stomach than the same dose of omeprazole.

That is a real difference in how the body handles the drug, but several widely cited trials compared 40 milligrams of the new product with 20 milligrams of the old one, and critics argued that much of the advantage could be had by simply raising the omeprazole dose.
I find it hard to read the esomeprazole episode as anything but a commercial achievement first and a scientific one a distant second.
It would be unfair to dismiss every switch on that basis.
Bupivacaine, a local anesthetic, is dangerous to the heart in overdose, and the danger is greater for its R enantiomer.
The S enantiomer, sold alone as levobupivacaine, provides comparable numbing with a wider margin of safety, which is exactly the sort of benefit the three-point model would predict.

A chiral switch is neither a scientific advance nor a marketing trick by definition; each one must be judged by whether patients do measurably better on the single enantiomer than on the mixture, at matched doses.
None of this should obscure how remarkable the underlying chemistry is.
Pasteur sorted crystals with tweezers because no other method existed.

Today chemists can build one enantiomer and not the other on an industrial scale using catalysts that are themselves chiral, work recognized by the 2001 Nobel Prize in Chemistry awarded to William Knowles, Ryoji Noyori, and Barry Sharpless.
For any new medicine it is now possible to ask which hand the body wants and to supply that hand alone.
Whether supplying it alone is worth paying for is a different question, and it should be answered by evidence rather than by the color of the pill.

questions.stem: According to the passage, what did Pasteur notice about the crystals of the sodium ammonium salt?
choices: They rotated light more strongly than tartaric acid did.
They were chemically different from ordinary tartaric acid.
They formed only when the solution was kept warm.
They could not be dissolved once they had been sorted.
They came in two mirror-image shapes.

proof.quote: noticed that they came in two shapes that were mirror images of each other

questions.why: Paragraph 2 says Pasteur, looking through a magnifying lens, noticed that the crystals came in two shapes that were mirror images of each other. That observation is the whole starting point of the passage.
distractorNotes: The crystals themselves were from the inactive acid; the passage says the solutions rotated light equally in opposite directions, not more strongly than tartaric acid.
Paragraph 2 says the inactive acid was chemically identical to tartaric acid in every test, the reverse of this choice.
The passage never mentions temperature or warming; this is outside the passage.
Paragraph 2 says he dissolved each pile after sorting, so this contradicts the text.

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT mentioned in the passage as part of Pasteur's work in 1848?
choices: heating the crystals to separate the two forms
crystallizing a sodium ammonium salt of the inactive acid
sorting the crystals by hand with tweezers
measuring the rotation produced by each solution
examining the crystals under a magnifying lens

proof.quote: crystallized a sodium ammonium salt of the inactive acid
With tweezers he sorted them into two piles
found that one solution rotated light to the right and the other to the left
examining the crystals under a magnifying lens

questions.why: Paragraph 2 confirms the salt, the lens, the tweezers, and the measured rotations, but it never mentions heating. The separation was done by eye and by hand, so heating is the one you cannot confirm.
distractorNotes: Paragraph 2 says Pasteur crystallized a sodium ammonium salt of the inactive acid.
Paragraph 2 says he sorted the crystals into two piles with tweezers.
Paragraph 2 says he found one solution rotated light to the right and the other to the left.
Paragraph 2 says he examined the crystals under a magnifying lens.

questions.stem: According to the passage, two enantiomers of the same compound differ in
choices: their melting points and boiling points
the direction they rotate polarized light
the number of stereocenters they each contain
their solubility and density in water
the strength of their bonds to carbon

proof.quote: in the direction they rotate polarized light

questions.why: Paragraph 4 lists exactly two circumstances in which enantiomers differ: the direction they rotate polarized light and how they interact with other chiral things. Everything else on this list is something they share.
distractorNotes: Paragraph 4 says enantiomers share the same melting point and boiling point.
Enantiomers are mirror images of the same molecule; the passage never says they differ in number of stereocenters.
Paragraph 4 says they share the same solubility and density.
Bond strength is never discussed; this is outside the passage.

questions.stem: As used in paragraph 5, the word "particular" most nearly means
choices: specific
individual
unusual
detailed
selective

proof.quote: as particular about shape as a glove

questions.why: Paragraph 5 calls a receptor a chiral pocket that is as particular about shape as a glove. A glove is choosy about which hand it accepts, so here "particular" means selective or fussy, not specific or individual.
distractorNotes: "Specific" is the common meaning of the word, but a glove is not specific about shape; it is choosy about shape.
"Individual" is another everyday sense of "particular" that does not fit a glove being picky.
Nothing in the sentence suggests the receptor is unusual; the comparison is about pickiness.
"Detailed" does not describe a glove's relationship to a hand.

questions.stem: According to the passage, the three-point attachment model explains why
choices: enzymes are built from amino acids of a single handedness
a drug's two enantiomers share the same melting point
receptors change shape when a drug binds to them
only one enantiomer can fully fit a receptor
the distomer of every drug is harmful to the body

proof.quote: only one enantiomer can line up all three at once, while its mirror image can manage two at best

questions.why: Paragraph 5 describes the model: if a drug must touch its receptor at three points, only one enantiomer can line up all three, while the mirror image manages two at best. The model is about fit, not about what the distomer does.
distractorNotes: That proteins are built from one-handed amino acids is stated earlier in the paragraph as a fact, not something the model explains.
Shared melting point is a physical property from paragraph 4, unrelated to the model.
The passage never says receptors change shape; this is outside the passage.
Paragraph 5 says a distomer may do nothing, something milder, something different, or harm; "every" is far too strong.

questions.stem: The author ends paragraph 5 with the words "may do harm" primarily to
choices: argue that racemic mixtures should never be approved for sale
introduce the thalidomide case that follows
explain why the body's proteins are one-handed
contrast ibuprofen's distomer with esomeprazole's
summarize the model proposed by Easson and Stedman

proof.quote: in the worst case, may do harm
The worst case has a name.

questions.why: The last line of paragraph 5 names the worst case a distomer can be, and paragraph 6 opens with "The worst case has a name" and tells the thalidomide story. The phrase is a bridge into that example.
distractorNotes: The author later praises racemic ibuprofen and asks for case-by-case judgment, so a blanket ban is far too strong.
One-handed proteins are explained at the start of paragraph 5, not by its closing words.
Ibuprofen and esomeprazole come in paragraphs 8 to 10, and the passage never contrasts their distomers.
The model is summarized in the third sentence; the closing sentence lists what a distomer can do, which goes beyond the model.

questions.stem: According to the passage, the United States was largely spared the thalidomide disaster because
choices: the drug was never manufactured or sold anywhere outside West Germany
American physicians connected it to birth defects before it went on sale
a 1962 law banned the use of sedatives during pregnancy
the drug's single-enantiomer form was the only version sold there
an FDA reviewer withheld approval over inadequate safety data

proof.quote: refused to approve the drug for lack of adequate safety data

questions.why: Paragraph 6 says Frances Kelsey, a reviewer at the FDA, refused to approve the drug for lack of adequate safety data. The 1962 law came afterward and strengthened the agency's demands; it was not the reason.
distractorNotes: Paragraph 6 says thousands of children were affected worldwide, so the drug was clearly sold beyond West Germany.
The passage credits an FDA reviewer, not American physicians, and says the drug was never approved there.
The 1962 law strengthened demands for evidence; the passage never says it banned sedatives in pregnancy, and it came after the refusal.
Paragraph 7 says a single-enantiomer version would not have been safe, and the passage never says one was sold anywhere.

questions.stem: The passage suggests that if thalidomide had been sold only as its sedative enantiomer,
choices: the harmful form would still have formed inside patients
the sedative effect would have been lost entirely
the FDA would have approved it for sale in 1957
the birth defects would have been prevented
the drug could not have returned for leprosy complications in 1998

proof.quote: either pure enantiomer turns into a mixture of both within hours of being swallowed
the body would have manufactured the harmful form on its own

questions.why: Paragraph 7 says either pure enantiomer turns into a mixture of both within hours, and that the body would have manufactured the harmful form on its own. So the sedative-only version would have become the dangerous mixture anyway.
distractorNotes: Nothing suggests the sedative effect disappears; the problem is that the harmful form reappears alongside it.
Kelsey's refusal was about missing safety data; the passage never ties FDA approval to which enantiomer was sold.
Paragraph 7 calls exactly this conclusion wrong.
The 1998 return is about strict controls for a leprosy complication; the passage never links it to the enantiomer sold.

questions.stem: Which of the following new situations best illustrates the problem described in paragraph 7?
choices: A heartburn drug whose two enantiomers become the same active molecule once acid converts them
A painkiller whose inactive enantiomer is steadily converted by the body into the active enantiomer over several hours
An antibiotic sold as one pure enantiomer that becomes a fifty-fifty mixture in patients' blood
A crystalline drug whose harmful enantiomer can be removed by sorting its crystals by hand
A fragrance compound whose two enantiomers produce entirely different smells

proof.quote: either pure enantiomer turns into a mixture of both within hours of being swallowed

questions.why: The problem in paragraph 7 is interconversion: a pure enantiomer turns into a mixture of both inside the body, so selling the safe hand alone does not help. An antibiotic that becomes a fifty-fifty mixture in the blood is the same situation with a new drug.
distractorNotes: Two enantiomers becoming one achiral active form is the omeprazole case from paragraph 10, not interconversion between enantiomers.
One-way conversion of the inactive form into the active one is the ibuprofen case from paragraph 8, which the passage presents as helpful rather than a problem.
Sorting crystals by hand is Pasteur's method from paragraph 2 and has nothing to do with what happens inside the body.
Different smells are the carvone example from paragraph 4, which illustrates that enantiomers interact differently with chiral things.

questions.stem: All of the following are stated in the passage about ibuprofen EXCEPT:
choices: It was developed at the Boots company in Britain.
Only its S enantiomer blocks the target enzyme.
The body converts part of the R form into the S form.
The conversion of R to S runs in both directions.
A pure S version is sold in some countries.

proof.quote: Developed at the Boots company in Britain in the 1960s
Only the S enantiomer blocks the enzyme
releases it as the active S form
A pure S version is sold in some countries
a conversion that runs in only one direction

questions.why: Paragraph 8 confirms Boots, the S enantiomer as the active one, the R-to-S conversion, and the pure S product, but it says the conversion runs in only one direction. A two-way conversion is the opposite of what the passage states.
distractorNotes: Paragraph 8 says ibuprofen was developed at the Boots company in Britain in the 1960s.
Paragraph 8 says only the S enantiomer blocks the enzyme behind pain and inflammation.
Paragraph 8 says the body inverts the R form and releases it as the active S form.
Paragraph 8 says a pure S version is sold in some countries.

questions.stem: According to the passage, the FDA's 1992 policy statement
choices: required that all new drugs be sold as single enantiomers
banned the sale of racemic mixtures in the United States
approved esomeprazole for sale as a new product
introduced the term chiral switch into the industry
encouraged separate study of each enantiomer

proof.quote: encouraging developers to study each enantiomer of a new chiral drug separately

questions.why: Paragraph 9 says the 1992 statement encouraged developers to study each enantiomer of a new chiral drug separately. Encouraging is softer than requiring, and the passage says nothing about bans.
distractorNotes: "Required" and "all" are too strong; the passage says the statement encouraged study of each enantiomer.
Racemic ibuprofen remains the standard according to paragraph 8, so no ban occurred.
Esomeprazole was approved in 2001, nine years later, and the policy statement is not credited with that approval.
The passage says the industry calls the maneuver a chiral switch; it never attributes the term to the FDA.

questions.stem: The passage suggests that if the liver broke down both enantiomers of omeprazole at the same rate,
choices: omeprazole would no longer act as a prodrug
esomeprazole would offer little or no advantage
esomeprazole would deliver more drug to the stomach than before
the active form of the drug would regain its stereocenter
the 40 milligram trials would have shown a larger effect

proof.quote: the two enantiomers become the same molecule
The difference lies in the liver, which breaks down the S enantiomer more slowly

questions.why: Paragraph 10 says the two enantiomers become the same molecule at the site of action and that the difference lies in the liver, which breaks down the S enantiomer more slowly. Take away the liver difference and nothing is left to separate the two drugs.
distractorNotes: Omeprazole is a prodrug because stomach acid activates it, according to paragraph 10; liver rates have nothing to do with that.
Reversed: esomeprazole delivers more drug only because it is broken down more slowly, so equal breakdown would remove that extra delivery.
The active form lacks a stereocenter because of what acid does to it, not because of the liver.
Outside the passage, and backwards: with no liver difference, the trials would have shown less advantage, not more.

questions.stem: According to the passage, critics of esomeprazole argued that
choices: a higher dose of omeprazole could match much of its advantage
it was broken down by the liver faster than omeprazole
it caused more side effects than the older drug
its patent protection had already expired before the drug was approved
it failed to reach the acid-secreting cells of the stomach

proof.quote: critics argued that much of the advantage could be had by simply raising the omeprazole dose

questions.why: Paragraph 10 says widely cited trials compared 40 milligrams of the new drug with 20 milligrams of the old one, and critics argued that much of the advantage could be had by simply raising the omeprazole dose.
distractorNotes: Reversed: paragraph 10 says the liver breaks down the S enantiomer more slowly, not faster.
Side effects are never mentioned; this is outside the passage.
It was omeprazole's patent that was running out, according to paragraph 9, not esomeprazole's.
Paragraph 10 says esomeprazole delivers somewhat more drug to the stomach, not less.

questions.stem: The author's attitude toward the esomeprazole chiral switch is best described as
choices: enthusiastic approval
neutral indifference
measured skepticism
outright hostility
puzzled confusion

proof.quote: a commercial achievement first and a scientific one a distant second
That is a real difference in how the body handles the drug, but

questions.why: The author grants that there is a real difference in how the body handles the drug, then calls the episode a commercial achievement first and a scientific one a distant second. Conceding the point and still doubting the value is measured skepticism.
distractorNotes: The author doubts the scientific value of the switch; nothing in paragraph 10 is enthusiastic.
An author who tells the reader to slow down and then renders a judgment is not indifferent.
Hostility is too strong; the author concedes a real difference and says in paragraph 11 that not every switch should be dismissed.
The author is not confused; the mechanism is laid out clearly and a verdict is given.

questions.stem: The author discusses bupivacaine in paragraph 11 primarily to
choices: illustrate how the liver breaks down enantiomers at different rates
argue that local anesthetics should always be sold as racemates
prove that the three-point attachment model is incorrect
show that some chiral switches deliver a real benefit
compare the sales of levobupivacaine with those of esomeprazole

proof.quote: It would be unfair to dismiss every switch on that basis.
provides comparable numbing with a wider margin of safety

questions.why: Paragraph 11 opens by saying it would be unfair to dismiss every switch, then offers levobupivacaine as a single enantiomer with a wider margin of safety. The example exists to balance the skepticism of paragraph 10.
distractorNotes: Liver metabolism is the omeprazole story in paragraph 10; paragraph 11 is about heart toxicity.
Reversed: the passage presents the single enantiomer, not the racemate, as the safer anesthetic.
Reversed: the passage says the benefit is exactly what the three-point model would predict.
Sales figures are given only for esomeprazole; the passage never compares the two products commercially.

questions.stem: It can be inferred from the passage that before the development of chiral catalysts,
choices: no method existed that could distinguish one enantiomer from the other
producing a single enantiomer at industrial scale was difficult
Pasteur's method of sorting crystals was used in factories
drugs were never sold as single enantiomers
racemic mixtures were considered unsafe by regulators

proof.quote: Pasteur sorted crystals with tweezers because no other method existed.
Today chemists can build one enantiomer and not the other on an industrial scale using catalysts that are themselves chiral

questions.why: Paragraph 12 contrasts Pasteur's tweezers, used because no other method existed, with today's chiral catalysts that build one enantiomer on an industrial scale. The natural inference is that industrial-scale production of one hand was hard before those catalysts.
distractorNotes: Too strong: paragraph 2 shows that polarized light could tell the two apart as early as 1848.
The passage never says Pasteur's hand-sorting was used in factories; this is outside the passage.
Too strong: the passage never says single-enantiomer drugs were impossible before the catalysts, only that producing them at scale is now possible.
Paragraph 9 says the 1992 statement encouraged separate study; nothing says regulators considered racemates unsafe.

questions.stem: Which of the following best expresses the main idea of the passage?
choices: Pasteur's discovery of mirror-image crystals was the most important event in the history of chemistry.
Chiral switches are marketing maneuvers that regulators should prohibit.
Handedness shapes how drugs act, but each single-enantiomer product must be judged on evidence.
Thalidomide and ibuprofen show that racemic drugs are always more dangerous than single enantiomers.
Enzymes and receptors are chiral because they are built from amino acids of a single handedness.

proof.quote: a matter of life and death, and later, a matter of marketing
each one must be judged by whether patients do measurably better on the single enantiomer than on the mixture
it should be answered by evidence rather than by the color of the pill

questions.why: Paragraph 1 frames handedness as a matter of life and death and later of marketing; paragraph 11 says each switch must be judged by whether patients do better; paragraph 12 closes by asking for evidence rather than the color of the pill. The passage is about handedness mattering and the value being an evidence question.
distractorNotes: Pasteur is the opening story, not the thesis, and the passage never ranks his discovery against all of chemistry.
Too strong: paragraph 11 says a switch is neither an advance nor a trick by definition, and the author praises levobupivacaine.
Reversed and too strong: racemic ibuprofen is presented as perfectly good, and "always" contradicts paragraph 11.
That is a supporting fact from paragraph 5, not the main idea of the whole passage.
